newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Inquiry body recommends Bangladesh stock reforms.
newsitem.headline: Inquiry body recommends Bangladesh stock reforms.

text.p: An inquiry committee that rocked Bangladesh's stock market by urging the arrest of 36 major players on charges of share manipulation has recommended sweeping reforms to avert a recurrence of wrongdoing.
The committee report, submitted to the government on March 27, said the Dhaka Stock Exchange (DSE) should switch to automated trading immediately.
It further recommended the number of DSE members should be raised from the present 195 in consultation with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), the market watchdog.

"Stock dealers should be allowed to act as stock brokers because there is often conflict of interest between stock-dealing and stock-broking," said the report, a copy of which was obtained by Reuters on Thursday.

Dhaka's chief metropolitan magistrate on Wednesday ordered the arrest of 36 brokers and company owners, including DSE chairman Imtiyaz Husain. A report by the four-member committee headed by professor Amirul Islam Chowdhury prompted the arrests.
Police said they immediately began hunting for the suspects, who the committee said were involved in "fraudulent activities" that had sent share prices soaring and then plunging.
Brokers said the impact of the legal action should be positive.
"There has been an initial shock in the market in the wake of the crackdown. But I am sure about its positive impact in the long run," broker Abdul Rashid told Reuters.
Redwanul Islam, a trader with Dastagir M. Adil & Co., said: "Let us hope for the best. The market may stabilise soon. We expect a better result from this new experience."

The committee said the "sponsors of listed companies should be prohibited from unloading their shares for at least two years from listing or from the date of commercial operation of concerned securities, whichever is earlier".
It said the "SEC should discourage issue of shares at a premium. If necessary, they may encourage issuance of bonus shares to the existing shareholders to bring at par."
However, the committee felt such an important issue needed careful study by an expert committee.

Some of the reforms suggested by the committee were already in place before March 27. They included allowing eight private sector merchant banks to issue and manage mutual funds and unit trusts, and a decision by the government in principle for setting up a "national stock exchange (NSE)".
The committee said the government should immediately publish an outline of the NSE for a national debate.
"The establishment of the NSE and adoption of central depository system (CDS) will remove the problems of the kerb market to a great extent," the report said.
"The SEC has to be strengthened both managerially and organisationally," it said.

The report criticised the SEC for its "delayed action" against the sharp rise of the stock market. "The SEC instead of taking direct action against the wrongdoers -- such as suspension of trading and cancelling licenses of brokers -- took measures of corrective nature, that too belatedly, which failed to produce any positive results."

"The SEC should have been more aggressive in taking punitive actions against the manipulators. Strong actions could have stopped the debacles at the earlier stage and at a lesser cost to the investors."
Day-to-day administration of the DSE should be handled by a chief executive officer, appointed by the stock exchange council and not the DSE chairman, the committee said.
